props.title: Rolling Thunder
props.initialSlug: Vietnam vet's brutal revenge against home invaders

sections.content: Rolling Thunder (1977) represents a pivotal moment in post-Vietnam revenge thrillers, written by Paul Schrader fresh off Taxi Driver (1976). William Devane's chilling performance as Major Charles Rane, a POW returning home only to face brutal violence, captures the psychological devastation of veterans in ways that influenced later films like First Blood (1982). The film's unflinching violence and moral ambiguity shocked audiences, while its exploration of trauma and alienation established a template for character-driven revenge narratives.

sections.content: The film's influence extends deep into modern revenge thrillers. John Wick (2014) echoes Rolling Thunder's precise action choreography and personal motivation, while Dead Man's Shoes (2004) mirrors its methodical pacing and psychological complexity. Director John Flynn's stripped-down approach influenced a generation of filmmakers, from Quentin Tarantino (who named his distribution company Rolling Thunder Pictures) to Jeremy Saulnier's Blue Ruin (2013).

The film's treatment of PTSD and homecoming predates and influences later Vietnam-focused works like Coming Home (1978) and The Deer Hunter (1978). Its raw portrayal of readjustment challenges broke new ground, showing the psychological cost of war without Hollywood glamorization. The partnership between Rane and Johnny Vohden (Tommy Lee Jones) explores the brotherhood of soldiers who can only truly connect with fellow veterans. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: Rolling Thunder's DNA appears in contemporary revenge films like Drive (2011) and You Were Never Really Here (2017), which share its minimalist dialogue and explosive violence punctuating long stretches of tension. The film's influence on character-driven action extends to The Man from Nowhere (2010) and Nobody (2021), showing how personal trauma can transform ordinary men into efficient killing machines.
